title: Streaming
objectives: accumulate chunks into a finished answer

steps.instruction: A long answer takes seconds. Where those seconds go decides how your app feels.
body: Without streaming: you wait for the last token, then render everything. Blank screen the whole time.
With streaming: the first words appear almost immediately and keep coming.
Remember A1.1. It writes one token at a time, so the early ones exist long before the last one.
steps.keypoint: The tokens were always arriving one at a time. Streaming just stops hiding that.

steps.instruction: The same answer, streamed. How many pieces?
steps.after: Three pieces. In a real app each one arrives a moment apart, and each one can be shown.
steps.why: Three. In a real app each one lands a moment after the last, and each one can be shown immediately.

steps.instruction: Step through the arrival. Watch what the user can see at each moment.

frames.note: Nothing yet. Without streaming, the user sits here for the whole reply.
First chunk lands. The user is already reading while the model is still writing.
Second chunk appends. It never replaces what is there, it adds to it.
Last chunk. Done at exactly the same moment the non-streamed version would have been.

steps.after: Same 0.9 seconds either way. One of them felt instant.
steps.keypoint: Streaming does not save time. It moves the waiting to after the reading starts.

steps.instruction: The pieces, joined back into the answer.
steps.after: Nothing between the pieces. They are cut mid-word, so any separator corrupts the text.
body: Nothing between them. They are cut mid-word, so any separator corrupts the text.

steps.instruction: One of these lines loses everything that arrived before it. Tap it.
steps.why: = replaces, += appends. That single missing character makes the answer flicker and lose its first half, and it is the most common streaming bug there is.

steps.instruction: Printing after every chunk. What does the middle line look like?
steps.after: Three snapshots of the same screen, a third of a second apart.
steps.why: Cut mid-word, and that is fine to show. It is not fine to count words in, or search for a closing brace in.

steps.instruction: Look closely at that middle line. Chunks do not respect words.
body: The screen showed "Paris is the ans" for a moment. That is normal and it is fine.
It is not fine if you are counting words, cutting at a length, or looking for a closing bracket.
Partial text is safe to show. It is not safe to reason about.
steps.keypoint: Show partial text. Never make a decision from it.

steps.instruction: There is a second reason to stream, and it has nothing to do with feel.
body: A long reply on a slow model can outlast a request timeout, and you lose the whole thing.
A stream is delivering the whole time, so nothing sits idle waiting to be cut off.
For anything long, streaming is the safer transport, not just the nicer one.
steps.keypoint: Long replies stream, or they risk timing out entirely.

steps.instruction: Total time from pressing send to the last word appearing. Streamed against not streamed?
steps.code:
const streamed = ai.stream({ model: "small", messages: [{ role: "user", content: "What is the capital of France?" }] });
const whole = ai.ask({ model: "small", messages: [{ role: "user", content: "What is the capital of France?" }] });
opts: Almost exactly the same, but streaming starts showing much sooner
Streaming is slower because of the extra pieces
steps.why: The model does identical work either way. The last token arrives at the same moment. All that changed is that the first token was shown instead of held.
steps.after: Perceived speed is not a trick. It is the honest difference between waiting and reading.
steps.keypoint: Same finish line. Very different wait.

steps.instruction: Deal each job into whether streaming helps it.

items.text: a chat reply a person reads
JSON you are about to parse
a long explanation of an error
a one-word tag for a note

steps.after: The rule: if a human reads it as it arrives, stream. If code eats it whole, wait.
steps.keypoint: Stream what people read. Wait for what code parses.

steps.instruction: That JSON case deserves its own sentence.
body: Half a JSON object is not JSON. It is a syntax error waiting for its other half.
You cannot parse it early, and you cannot show it, so streaming buys nothing.
Ask for it whole, parse it once.
steps.keypoint: Never stream something you are going to parse.

steps.after: Accumulated, complete, and measurable. That is the whole streaming pattern.
body: That is the whole streaming pattern: append every chunk, use the result only when it is done.
